title: The Chimera Curriculum — K through PhD, hyper-focused on game development
commissioned: 2026-07-12 — 'the entire education system... hundreds of checkpoints... conceptualize a feature from every angle of humanity... like training an AI, if an AI was one feature'
note: Grow this file, never the engine. Each checkpoint = one angle of humanity applied to the carried feature. Verifiers are mechanical (core/curriculum.py); prompts lay out where the path runs — the agent makes the connections.

checkpoints.prompt: In ONE sentence a child would understand: what is fun about <feature>? Then run the toy test: describe what a player would do with it for 60 seconds if there were NO goal, NO reward, NO instructions — just the thing itself. If the honest answer is 'nothing', write that, and name what's missing.
What face does the player make the first time <feature> works — surprise, grin, narrowed-eye focus, relief? Name the exact on-screen event that causes that face IN THE SAME SECOND it happens.
Why does the player do <feature> a SECOND time? Name the itch — curiosity, mastery, greed, rhythm — and what the first use planted to cause it.

What NOUN does the player see or hold, and what VERB does <feature> give them? A verb needs behavior, not metadata (the shovel had DigRadius but no Dig). Name the exact input that fires the verb and the world-state change that proves it fired.
Explain <feature> twice: once in one sentence to a 10-year-old, once in one sentence to a senior designer. If the two sentences disagree about what it IS, the feature is confused — say so.
What is <feature> NOT? Name its nearest-neighbor feature (in Chimera or any game) that it must never be confused with, and the one distinction that keeps them apart.

What does the player SEE or HEAR that proves <feature> exists? Verified-by-injection is not playable — if the only proof lives in a log line or a debug command, this checkpoint fails on honesty. Describe the on-screen/in-ear evidence.
Describe the SMALLEST playable slice of <feature> that could ship today: one noun, one verb, one piece of feedback. What does the full version add that the smallest one already proves?
Name THREE shipped games that have <feature> (or its closest ancestor). One line each: what their version did well, what it did poorly. Bullet them.
Where does <feature> sit in Chimera: which spiral Loop, which board task (tb-id if one exists), and which player fantasy from the game's spine does it serve — astronaut, trader, explorer, survivor?

bands.title: Middle School — How does it feel?

checkpoints.prompt: Script the first 10 seconds of touching <feature>: the input, the response latency (a NUMBER — ms or frames), the visual acknowledgment, the audio acknowledgment. If any link in that chain is missing today, mark it MISSING.

Is <feature> readable at walk height against regolith-grey? Describe its silhouette, palette, and contrast strategy — the tri-pads already taught us surfaces can read uniformly void-black in situ. How does this feature avoid that fate?

Define <feature>'s sound signature: the source (what physically makes the noise), the trigger (what event fires it), its mix priority against footsteps and wind — and name one moment where SILENCE is the better choice.

List <feature>'s exact input bindings (keys/buttons/axes) and defend why each matches the verb's energy (a dig should feel heavier than a glance). Name any modifier-key traps — the Shift-modifier class has already burned a beat.
Which forgiveness mechanisms does <feature> need: input buffering, coyote time, cancel windows, sticky targeting? Pick what applies, give each a NUMBER (ms or frames), and name one it must NOT have.

Name <feature>'s feedback in all three channels — visual, audio, kinesthetic (camera/motion) — and for EACH: what the player loses if that channel is missing. A feature with one channel is a feature with one point of failure.
How does FAILURE feel in <feature> without a tooltip? Design the diegetic 'no': what the world does (sound, motion, material) to tell the player it didn't work and hint at why.
Name ONE cheap juice addition for <feature> (particles, pitch variance, screen-shake, hit-stop) and — harder — the exact point where more juice becomes noise for this feature.

bands.title: High School — How does it work?

checkpoints.prompt: Write <feature>'s loop in words: trigger -> player action -> resource delta -> state change -> what re-arms the trigger. If the loop doesn't close (nothing re-arms), say what external system must feed it.

Bullet THREE edge cases for <feature> — the zero-state (first use, nothing owned), the spam case (player mashes it), and one boundary value — and the INTENDED behavior for each. Undefined behavior is a design decision made by a compiler.
What information does <feature> HIDE from the player and what does it REVEAL? Defend one hidden thing: why does concealment serve play here rather than frustrate it?

Write <feature>'s governing formula or curve with REAL numbers plugged in — growth rate, decay, threshold, cooldown, whatever rules it. Two worked values minimum: the typical case and the extreme case.

Name the THREE tuning knobs a designer gets on <feature>, each with its sane range (numbers) and what breaks outside the range. A feature with no knobs cannot be balanced; one with ten cannot be understood.

Where does randomness live in <feature>, if anywhere? State the expected value of a typical interaction AND the worst case a player can hit through no fault of their own. If deterministic, defend why determinism is right here.

List <feature>'s physical quantities with UNITS (UE units, m/s, kg-equivalents) and what integrates per tick. Name one place where frame-rate dependence could corrupt it and how it stays deterministic.

What does <feature> COST the player (time, attention, resources, risk) and what does it PAY? State the exchange rate with at least one number. An interaction that costs nothing teaches nothing — the sacrifice log is watching.

Decompose <feature> into UE classes/components: what owns what, what attaches where. For EACH file, declare generator-owned vs loop-built manual (the Contract: hand-edits to generator-owned files are clobbered on the next pipeline run).

Bullet the top THREE engineering failure modes for <feature> (missing attachment, silent default, template drift, lock contention...) and name the mandatory gate (gate_*) or heuristic that catches each.

Make <feature>'s lifecycle decisions: what happens at BeginPlay, what ticks (and what must NOT tick), attachment/initialization ORDER. The telemetry-defaults class of bug (count=0, latency=999) is an initialization-order corpse — how does this feature avoid joining it?

Write the exact MCP read-back that proves <feature> is alive in PIE: tool, action, property, EXPECTED value. Read back live pawn components before staging any interaction verb — a component never attached is a feature never built.

Trace <feature>'s data: where its parameters come from (the DSL spec block or a manual config), which UPROPERTYs expose them, what enters the save game, and what is derived-at-runtime and must NEVER be saved.

Declare <feature>'s performance budget: fps floor, memory ceiling, actor/particle counts — NUMBERS — and how you will measure them FOREGROUNDED (background throttle freezes fps AND all Niagara/anim simulation; a backgrounded measurement is a lie).

Sketch <feature>'s beat script: which REGISTERED sleepwalker actions it uses (beats declaring unregistered actions fail at dispatch), which schema-bound expects verify it, and where reset_position must fire (W-drift accumulates across sequential beats).

Which of <feature>'s telemetry values could LIE by defaulting (the count=0 / latency=999 class means the backend component isn't populating, not that the world is quiet)? For each lying default: the read-back that exposes the lie.

Consult ONE live online source about <feature>'s craft (GDC talk, engine docs, postmortem, technical blog). Cache a copy on disk (research_corpus/ or docs/research/) — retrieval leaves evidence. Cite the URL, the cache path, and ONE number you extracted that changes how this feature should be built.

bands.title: Master's — How does it fit? (every angle of humanity)

checkpoints.prompt: Quote the STORY_BIBLE phrase or Design Law that <feature> serves, self-score its vision_fit (0.2-1.5, one decimal), and defend the score in three sentences. If it serves no phrase, score it honestly and say what that means.
checkpoints.calibration_note: 2026-07-12 first full run: was require_numeric, but vision_fit is a bare multiplier — the number-with-unit vocabulary (fps/ms/%) punished the checkpoint's own subject. Score pattern matched directly instead.

checkpoints.prompt: Run <feature> through the art bible: how does it live inside regolith-grey resonant minimalism without disappearing into it? Name the exact condition under which it would read void-black at walk height, and the check that catches that before a player sees it.

Design one WORDLESS narrative micro-moment <feature> can host — a moment where using it says something about this world or this astronaut, with zero text. What does the player understand afterward that they didn't before?

Connect <feature> to the sacrifice economy and the Costless Life failure ending: does using it ever COST something that the sacrifice log should remember? If it refuses that connection, defend the refusal — not every feature must carry the theme, but every feature must know where it stands.

Give <feature> one concrete accommodation per lens — visual (low vision / colorblind), motor (one-handed / low precision), cognitive (memory / attention), auditory (deaf / hard of hearing). Bullet all four. 'It's fine as-is' fails unless you prove the lens is genuinely untouched.

Run the cultural and ethical pass on <feature>: what could exclude, stereotype, or harm; where it touches player trust (fake urgency, dark patterns, hidden odds); the line it must never cross even if metrics reward crossing it.

Chart <feature>'s emotion across mastery: hour one (discovery) versus hour ten (fluency). Where does boredom set in, and what does the feature reveal or escalate to answer it? Name the emotion you are DESIGNING FOR, not just the one you hope for.

The player has a body: assess <feature> for motion sickness (camera acceleration, FOV changes), photosensitivity (flash frequency), and fatigue (hold-to-repeat strain, reach on the keyboard). Name its riskiest bodily interaction and the mitigation.
Name TWO other live Chimera systems <feature> interacts with (movement, economy, sound, tools, save...). For each: the interaction, one EXPLOIT a hostile player finds at the seam, and its fix.

Place <feature> in L_RegolithYard: where it lives, what landmark makes it findable, the sightline that teaches it before the player touches it, and what its placement says about how often the designer expects it used.

Set <feature> against TWO titles from the benchmark pool (Elite Dangerous, No Man's Sky, Star Citizen, EVE Online, Subnautica): where Chimera's version stands, one thing it deliberately steals, one thing it deliberately refuses — bullet per title.

The coherence exam: connect at least THREE of <feature>'s own earlier schoolwork artifacts (cite their filenames) into ONE design stance — show that kindergarten's fun, high school's math, and bachelor's engineering describe the SAME feature, or name the contradiction you found.

bands.title: PhD — Prove it deserves to exist

checkpoints.prompt: Write <feature>'s exam: at least TWO numeric acceptance criteria, each with a citation — one from a LIVE online source (URL + on-disk cached copy; retrieval leaves evidence) and at least two on-disk sources total. Research writes the exam; the exam is numbers.

Present the sleepwalker's testimony: a SimPlaytest in the graph must name <feature> in its outcomes. Quote the outcome honestly (reached/failed/blocked) and use the NEWEST simtest — an old simtest can indict a feature already fixed since.

Report <feature>'s measured numbers against its declared bachelor-band budget: fps vs floor, crash-free soak duration, growth. State HOW it was measured (foregrounded, per the telemetry law) and whether each number passes its own budget.

The feature's implementation task must have exited the board `done` with real evidence — through the single entry, inside its footprint. Cite the task id and quote its recorded result in the artifact.

The defense, >=600 characters: claim -> evidence -> verdict. State what <feature> claims to give the player; marshal the evidence (cite one H-rule, one graph node id or argue 'no prior', TWO of your own earlier artifacts by filename, and one benchmark title); end with a verdict — PROCEED, REFINE, or PARK — and what would change your mind.

State <feature>'s falsifiable claim: 'if MEASUREMENT misses THRESHOLD, this feature is wrong and should be reworked.' One sentence, with a real number. If you cannot write this sentence, the feature is a belief, not a design.

Write what the NEXT feature inherits from <feature>'s schooling: TWO lessons, each concrete enough to be a surprise or heuristic record. If you already recorded them to the graph, cite the node ids; if not, argue 'no prior' and record them before the next enrollment.
